newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Retailers hold key to success of euro - economist.
newsitem.headline: Retailers hold key to success of euro - economist.

text.p: Retailers hold the key to the successful launch of the euro currency, David Croughan, chief economist of the Irish Business and Employers Confederation (IBEC) said on Thursday.

"Even more than banks, the retail sector will be the pillars of confidence for the consumer, because it is only when the consumer actually spends the euro, as opposed to obtaining it, that he/she will start to learn about its value," he told a workshop after IBEC's annual conference.
He said the retail sector would also hold a key role in withdrawing the currency the euro replaced and its views on the timing of the introduction of notes and coins should be given due weight.

"The more prepared the consumer is for the euro, the less confused he/she will be when euro pricing appears in the shops and the less will be the problems that the retail sector has to overcome," he said.
Croughan told delegates the onus was on governments to produce, with the help of communications specialists, a clear changeover plan which the public could understand.
Government departments and public utilities could also begin dual pricing displays of key amounts to help prepare the public for the changeover, he said.
Banks should display final balances in both currencies on statements and on the slips issued by cash dispensers, he said.
Croughan argued that the period in which both the euro and national currency were in circulation should not be longer than one month, although each EU government could decide.
The period of October to February for introducing the new currency had been ruled out because of the consumer boom around Christmas time and during the January sales, he said.
Croughan argued that the introduction of the new currency should be in March 2001 rather than in March 2002 becase "a three-year transition period is too long".

"Any extension runs counter to the original intentions where the words 'January 2002 at the latest' carried with it strong implications that the transition period would be shorter than the three-year scenario," he said.
Croughan called for the maximum information campaign possible with leaflets and posters made available and conversion tables printed at banks and other key outlets.
Dual pricing, wherever possible, would also help smoothe the transition although it would be difficult to carry out on small objects such as cosmetics, he said.
